sections.html:
A Vermont bill has two layers: a statewide education tax and a municipal tax set by each town. The town listers set the appraised value on the grand list, and the town collects both parts.

The Department of Taxes, through its Property Valuation and Review division, oversees the system. With 247 municipalities, 237 towns and 10 cities, the bill depends heavily on where the house sits. The state sets the education rate framework, while your selectboard and voters set the municipal side.

MeasureRate or ratio
Statewide common level of appraisal72.36 percent
Nonhomestead education tax rate1.391 percent
Homestead education base rate1.00 percent
Effective total rate, homestead1.66 percent
Effective total rate, nonhomestead1.70 percent

The common level of appraisal compares listed value with fair market value. At 72.36 percent, a typical house sells for more than its listed value, and the state uses that ratio to adjust education rates. It does not change the value on your own bill.

By filing a homestead declaration you tell the state this house is your domicile, and you pay the homestead education rate rather than the nonhomestead rate. Without a declaration, Vermont treats the property as nonhomestead.

The declaration is due each April 15, with October 15 as the last accepted date. A town can charge a late penalty of up to 3 percent if the nonhomestead rate is higher than the homestead rate, or up to 8 percent if it is lower. After the October deadline the property is classified as nonhomestead, and the owner pays the higher rate plus any penalty and interest.

  • As a rule you must be a Vermont resident living in your own home as a domicile on April 1.
  • A home leased more than 182 days in the calendar year, used exclusively for commercial or rental purposes, or used as a second home or camp is nonhomestead.
  • A home sold before April 1 generally can't carry a homestead declaration.

The same Form HS-122 carries the property tax credit claim. About two-thirds of homesteads receive a credit, and households with income under $47,000 may get an additional credit and a municipal credit.

You appeal in steps, starting with the town listers, then the board of civil authority, then the state or the Superior Court. Each step has a short deadline.

  1. Listers hear people aggrieved by their appraisals on or before May 20, and such hearings are not held later than June 2 (32 V.S.A. § 4221).
  2. After the listers' final decision, appeal in writing to the board of civil authority within 14 days after the date of notice, by lodging the appeal with the town clerk (32 V.S.A. § 4404).
  3. From the board's decision, an appeal to the Director of Property Valuation and Review or the Superior Court begins by notice within 30 days (32 V.S.A. § 4461).

The board of civil authority must hold a hearing and inspect each appealed parcel, and it may sustain, increase or decrease the listers' value. Few cases reach the state level: 36 appeals on the 2023 grand list and 19 on the 2024 grand list.

Many towns are overdue, and the state is pushing them toward regular reappraisals. Act 68 requires full reappraisals every six years starting January 1, 2025, unless the Division approves a longer period.

The average last reappraisal year across the state is 2016, and 60 towns last reappraised more than 15 years ago. Towns have been booking reappraisals for 2026 through 2029.

A reappraisal can move the listed value closer to market value. Before you assume your tax bill matches what a buyer will pay, check the date of your town's last reappraisal on the town website or ask the listers.

The state projects that the average education property tax bill will rise by 11.9 percent in fiscal year 2027.

That percentage is a statewide average, so individual bills vary. Homestead rates depend on local education spending, and the nonhomestead rate is uniform statewide. Buyers reading the bill on a listing sheet may be looking at last year's number, so show the current bill from the town clerk or treasurer.

sections.h2: Current Use and what it means for a seller
sections.html:
Current Use, formally the Use Value Appraisal program, taxes enrolled farm and forest land on its productive use value instead of market value. It started in 1978 and now covers 19,692 parcels and 2,574,742 acres, about one-third of Vermont's land.

  • Enrolled land stays in the program after a sale unless the owner or the Division withdraws it.
  • The new owner must submit a transfer application and required documents within 30 days after the transfer is recorded.
  • Once an application is approved and recorded, a contingent lien is placed on the land.
  • If the new owner develops the land or changes its use, the land use change tax may apply, at 10 percent of the fair market value of developed land.

The 2024 use values were $188 an acre for forest land, $141 an acre for forest more than one mile from a road, and $483 an acre for agricultural land. A house on a larger wooded lot may be partly enrolled, so ask your listers whether any of your acreage is in the program before you list.

Closing brings one main tax, the property transfer tax, payable within 30 days of the closing date. A buyer who will live in the house pays 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 and 1.25 percent beyond it, with a 0.22 percent Clean Water Surcharge on the portion over $200,000. A year-round home that won't be the buyer's principal residence and isn't a long-term rental carries 3.40 percent, or 3.62 percent with the surcharge.

Sellers who live out of state see 2.5 percent of the price withheld by the buyer, who files Form RW-171 within 30 days, unless the seller holds a Commissioner's Certificate.

Expect $15.00 per page to record a deed and a flat $15.00 for a transfer tax return. The town clerk has the current figures.

sections.h2: Selling with back property tax owed
sections.html:
Owing tax doesn't stop a Vermont sale: the unpaid amount comes out of the proceeds at closing. It still helps to know how collection works before you pick a closing date.

  • A collector may charge a commission of up to 8 percent of the tax after the deadline in the collector's notice, and voters may set a lower rate or a grace period (32 V.S.A. § 1674).
  • The collector mails a notice at least 30 days before the payment date, and if no date is set payment is due 30 days after mailing (32 V.S.A. § 4772).
  • A tax sale needs a delinquency of at least $1,500 for more than one year, and the collector must first offer a written repayment plan (32 V.S.A. § 5252).
  • The sale is advertised in a local newspaper three weeks in a row, and the delinquent owner and any mortgagee get certified-mail notice at least 30 days before the sale.

After a tax sale the owner, lienholder or mortgagee may redeem within one year by paying the sale price plus interest at 1 percent per month. Landlords selling a rental should also know that owners of rented property file a Landlord Certificate (Form LRC-140) each year.

If the back taxes are tied to a house you can't afford to fix up, an as-is cash sale can pay them off at closing.

faqs.q: When is the Vermont homestead declaration due?
faqs.a: Each April 15, with October 15 as the last accepted date. After that, the property is classified as nonhomestead and the owner pays the higher rate plus any penalty.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Vermont assessment to the board of civil authority?
faqs.a: You have 14 days after the date of the listers' notice, and you lodge the appeal in writing with the town clerk under 32 V.S.A. § 4404.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Vermont if I owe property taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, the unpaid tax is paid from the proceeds at closing. A tax sale requires at least $1,500 delinquent for more than a year, and owners get a year to redeem.

faqs.q: Does a nonresident seller owe Vermont withholding?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer withholds 2.5 percent of the sale price on Form RW-171 unless the seller holds a Commissioner's Certificate.

faqs.q: What is the Vermont property transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: For a principal residence it is 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 and 1.25 percent above, plus a 0.22 percent surcharge on the excess. Many non-principal homes pay 3.40 percent.
